meta.title: Burmese B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Burmese → English (see the Burmese, recall the meaning) and English → Burmese (see an English meaning, recall the Burmese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Burmese, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 111 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the written language (the literary particles a reader meets first), health, work and money, study, the media, the environment, society, the law and conflict, opinions, feelings, travel, the home and the neighbours, change and doing things, and describing — and the other 889 are the commonest remaining words of the Burmese Wikipedia. Burmese writes no spaces between words, so that text was cut into words against the dictionary, and only words of two syllables or more are taken from the count (a one-syllable count also holds every piece the cut could not place). Burmese has two registers, the written and the spoken. This level begins with the WRITTEN one: the literary particles and words (သည်, ၏, နှင့်, ဤ, ထို) that the A1 and A2 decks leave out and that a reader of a newspaper or a notice meets on every line; its fill is the written language of the Burmese Wikipedia, encyclopaedic in places (government, history, religion). English Wiktionary has fewer of this level's everyday words, so the vocabulary written for the level is short and the commonest remaining words are most of it. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here. Every word is in the Myanmar script, as Burmese is written; the Alphabet deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters and the tone marks. Beneath each word is its pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, as Wiktionary gives it, with the four tones marked: à low, á high, a̰ creaky, aʔ checked (short, with a catch). Many short Burmese words are several words in one spelling, so a card shows the meanings of the part of speech it teaches (ကို, the object particle; ငါး, five and fish). A noun shows the classifier it is counted with where Wiktionary names one. Example sentences are few: 83 of the 1000 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 590 Burmese sentences; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have a Burmese voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, pronunciation and classifiers: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Burmese Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
